question: What is content negotiation in Spring MVC?
title: Content Negotiation in Spring MVC — Accept and Content-Type Headers
direct_answer: **Content negotiation** is the process where the client and server agree on the format of data exchanged. The client sends `Accept: application/json` to indicate what it wants in the response. The server selects the appropriate `HttpMessageConverter` (Jackson for JSON, JAXB for XML) to produce that format.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of HTTP content negotiation mechanism
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Content-Type (request body format) with Accept (desired response format)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain both directions: Accept controls response format; Content-Type describes request body format

sections.title: Content Negotiation Flow
sections.content:
```
Request: GET /api/users/1
         Accept: application/json
                 ↓
         Spring checks: which MessageConverter produces application/json?
                 ↓
         MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter selected
                 ↓
Response: {"id":1,"name":"Alice"}
          Content-Type: application/json

Request: GET /api/users/1
         Accept: application/xml
                 ↓
         Spring: which converter produces application/xml? (needs jackson-dataformat-xml)
                 ↓
Response: <user><id>1</id><name>Alice</name></user>
```

sections.title: Content Negotiation Key Points
sections.content:
- **`Accept` header**: Client tells server what format it wants in the response
- **`Content-Type` header**: Client tells server what format it's sending in the request body
- **Server selects**: Spring iterates registered `HttpMessageConverter`s to find one that can produce the Accept type
- **`406 Not Acceptable`**: No registered converter can produce what the client wants
- **`415 Unsupported Media Type`**: Server can't read the Content-Type sent by client
- **JSON default**: Spring Boot auto-configures Jackson → JSON is default if Accept header is missing
- **XML support**: Add `jackson-dataformat-xml` dependency to support `application/xml`
- **`produces` attribute**: `@GetMapping(produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)` — restrict what this endpoint produces
- **`consumes` attribute**: `@PostMapping(consumes = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)` — restrict what this endpoint accepts

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Content negotiation is how the client and server agree on the data format. The client sends an Accept header saying what format it wants — like Accept: application/json. Spring looks through its registered HttpMessageConverters to find one that can produce that format. If Jackson is on the classpath, MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter handles JSON. If you add the jackson-dataformat-xml dependency, it can also produce XML. There are two directions here: the Accept header controls what format the response is in, and the Content-Type header tells the server what format the request body is in. If the server can't produce the requested format, it returns 406 Not Acceptable. You can also restrict endpoints to specific formats using the produces and consumes attributes on @GetMapping and @PostMapping.

question: What is the produces attribute in @GetMapping?
title: produces Attribute in @GetMapping — Restricting Response Content Type
direct_answer: The **`produces`** attribute on `@GetMapping` (and other mapping annotations) restricts which response content types this endpoint can produce. If the client's `Accept` header doesn't match any `produces` value, Spring returns `406 Not Acceptable` before even reaching the controller method.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of endpoint-level content type constraints
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing produces exists — thinking Spring auto-selects based on Accept header globally
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both produces and consumes together on a POST endpoint

sections.title: produces and consumes
produces vs consumes
sections.content:
- **`produces`**: Controls response format — matched against client's `Accept` header
- **`consumes`**: Controls request body format — matched against client's `Content-Type` header
- **`MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE`** = `"application/json"` — use constants for type safety
- **`MediaType.APPLICATION_XML_VALUE`** = `"application/xml"`
- **406 Not Acceptable**: produces value doesn't match client's Accept
- **415 Unsupported Media Type**: consumes value doesn't match client's Content-Type
- **Class level**: `@RequestMapping(produces=...)` at class level applies to all methods
- **Without produces**: Spring uses content negotiation to pick from all registered converters
- **When to use**: API versioning by content type, explicit documentation of endpoint capabilities

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The produces attribute on mapping annotations restricts the response formats your endpoint can produce. If you add produces=application/json, and a client sends Accept: application/xml, Spring returns 406 Not Acceptable without even calling your method. There's a partner attribute called consumes that restricts what request body formats your endpoint accepts — if a client sends Content-Type: text/plain and your endpoint has consumes=application/json, they get 415 Unsupported Media Type. These attributes are useful for being explicit about your API's contract, and they're particularly useful for API versioning by content type — where different versions of the API produce different media types. Without specifying produces, Spring uses global content negotiation to pick the best available converter.

question: How does Spring Boot auto-configure JSON support?
title: Spring Boot JSON Auto-Configuration — Jackson and ObjectMapper
direct_answer: Spring Boot auto-configures JSON support through `JacksonAutoConfiguration` when `jackson-databind` is on the classpath. It creates a default `ObjectMapper` bean, registers `MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter`, and sets `application/json` as the default produced content type for `@RestController` methods.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Spring Boot auto-configuration for JSON
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that spring-boot-starter-web already includes Jackson — trying to add it separately
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how to customize ObjectMapper with application.properties or a @Bean

sections.title: Jackson Auto-Configuration
sections.content:
When `spring-boot-starter-web` is added:
1. `jackson-databind` is transitively included
2. `JacksonAutoConfiguration` activates
3. A default `ObjectMapper` bean is created
4. `MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter` is registered with the ObjectMapper
5. All `@RestController` return values → Jackson JSON serialization

No extra configuration needed for basic JSON support.

sections.title: Jackson Customization
sections.content:
- **Via properties**: Configure ObjectMapper behavior without code:
  ```properties
  spring.jackson.serialization.indent-output=true
  spring.jackson.serialization.write-dates-as-timestamps=false
  spring.jackson.deserialization.fail-on-unknown-properties=false
  spring.jackson.default-property-inclusion=NON_NULL
  ```
- **Via @Bean**: `@Bean ObjectMapper objectMapper()` — full control, replaces default
- **Via `Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer`**: Customize without replacing default bean
- **`@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown=true)`**: On DTO class — ignore unknown JSON fields during deserialization
- **Module registration**: `JavaTimeModule` for Java 8 date/time serialization (often auto-registered)
- **`spring-boot-starter-web`**: Brings `jackson-databind`, `jackson-core`, `jackson-annotations` transitively

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Spring Boot auto-configures JSON through JacksonAutoConfiguration, which activates when jackson-databind is on the classpath — it's already included when you use spring-boot-starter-web. It creates a default ObjectMapper bean and registers it with a MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter, so any @RestController method returning a Java object automatically gets JSON serialization. You can customize the ObjectMapper behavior through application.properties — things like indenting the output, not serializing null fields, or using ISO date format instead of timestamps. For deeper customization, you can define your own ObjectMapper bean, though using Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer is gentler since it lets you add to the auto-configured settings rather than replacing them entirely.

question: What is MediaType in Spring MVC?
title: MediaType in Spring MVC — Content Type Constants
direct_answer: **`MediaType`** is a Spring class containing constants for MIME type strings used in `produces`, `consumes`, and `Content-Type` headers. Key constants: `MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE` = `"application/json"`, `MediaType.APPLICATION_XML_VALUE`, `MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN_VALUE`, `MediaType.MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of MediaType constants as best practice over string literals
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using hardcoded strings like 'application/json' instead of MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention MediaType can be parsed, compared, and checked for compatibility

sections.title: MediaType Constants
Common MediaType Constants
sections.content:
- **`APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE`** = `"application/json"` — REST API default
- **`APPLICATION_XML_VALUE`** = `"application/xml"` — XML responses
- **`TEXT_PLAIN_VALUE`** = `"text/plain"` — plain text
- **`TEXT_HTML_VALUE`** = `"text/html"` — HTML responses
- **`MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE`** = `"multipart/form-data"` — file uploads
- **`APPLICATION_FORM_URLENCODED_VALUE`** = form submissions
- **`APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM_VALUE`** = binary data / file downloads
- **`MediaType` object vs `_VALUE` String**: `MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON` is the object; `APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE` is the String constant
- **Best practice**: Use constants to avoid typos and IDE auto-complete support

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: MediaType is a Spring class that provides constants for MIME type strings. Instead of hardcoding 'application/json' as a string — which is error-prone — you use MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE, which is just a String constant. There are two forms: the MediaType object itself — like MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON — which you use when calling methods like HttpHeaders.setContentType(); and the _VALUE string variant — MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE — which you use in annotation attributes like produces and consumes. Common ones to know: APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE for REST APIs, MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE for file uploads, APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM_VALUE for binary file downloads. Using constants avoids typos and makes code more readable.

question: What is the difference between Content-Type and Accept HTTP headers?
title: Content-Type vs Accept HTTP Headers — Request and Response Format
direct_answer: **`Content-Type`** describes the format of the **request body** being sent by the client. **`Accept`** tells the server what format the client wants in the **response**. Example: `POST /users` with `Content-Type: application/json` (I'm sending JSON) and `Accept: application/json` (I want JSON back).

interviewer_intent.testing: Common HTTP header confusion — frequently asked in interviews
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mixing up Content-Type and Accept — saying Content-Type controls the response format
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the direction: Content-Type describes what's being sent; Accept describes what's wanted back

sections.title: Content-Type vs Accept Direction
sections.content:
```
POST /api/users
Content-Type: application/json  ← "I'm sending JSON in the body"
Accept: application/json         ← "I want JSON in the response"

Body: {"name": "Alice", "email": "alice@example.com"}

Server reads Content-Type → uses Jackson to DESERIALIZE request body
Server reads Accept → uses Jackson to SERIALIZE response body
Server sends:
Content-Type: application/json
Body: {"id":1,"name":"Alice","email":"alice@example.com"}
```

sections.title: Header Comparison
sections.content:
| Header | Direction | Meaning | Spring maps to |
|--------|-----------|---------|---------------|
| `Content-Type` | Client → Server | Format of request body | `@RequestBody` deserialization |
| `Accept` | Client → Server | Desired response format | `@ResponseBody` serialization |
| `Content-Type` (response) | Server → Client | Format of response body | Set by Spring automatically |

- **Missing Accept**: Spring uses default (usually JSON if Jackson configured)
- **Missing Content-Type on POST**: May cause `HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException` (400)
- **consumes matches Content-Type**: Spring's `consumes` attribute checks incoming Content-Type
- **produces matches Accept**: Spring's `produces` attribute checks incoming Accept header

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Content-Type and Accept serve different purposes in HTTP. Content-Type is about what's being sent — the client sets it on a POST or PUT request to tell the server what format the request body is in, like Content-Type: application/json. The server also sets it on the response to tell the client what format the response body is in. Accept is about what the client wants back — the client sets it to express its preferred response format, like Accept: application/json. So in a typical REST call: the client sends Content-Type: application/json to say 'I'm sending JSON', and Accept: application/json to say 'please send me JSON back'. In Spring, Content-Type is used by @RequestBody deserialization, and Accept is used by @ResponseBody serialization to pick the right HttpMessageConverter.

question: How do you add XML support to a Spring Boot REST API?
title: XML Support in Spring Boot REST API — jackson-dataformat-xml
direct_answer: Add the **`jackson-dataformat-xml`** dependency to your `pom.xml`. Spring Boot auto-detects it and registers `MappingJackson2XmlHttpMessageConverter`. Then your `@RestController` methods can serve both JSON (`Accept: application/json`) and XML (`Accept: application/xml`) automatically.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of multi-format support in Spring REST
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking XML requires @XmlRootElement (JAXB) — Jackson's XML module works without JAXB annotations
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that jackson-dataformat-xml uses Jackson annotations you already have, not separate JAXB annotations

sections.title: Adding XML Support
sections.content:
```xml
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.dataformat</groupId>
    <artifactId>jackson-dataformat-xml</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

That's it! Spring Boot auto-configures:
- `MappingJackson2XmlHttpMessageConverter` registered
- Client sends `Accept: application/json` → gets JSON response
- Client sends `Accept: application/xml` → gets XML response
- Same controller method, same return type — Spring selects format automatically

sections.title: XML Support Details
sections.content:
- **One dependency**: `jackson-dataformat-xml` — Spring Boot handles the rest
- **Jackson annotations work**: `@JsonProperty`, `@JsonIgnore` work for both JSON and XML
- **XML-specific**: `@JacksonXmlRootElement(localName='user')` — customize root element name
- **`@JacksonXmlProperty`**: Customize XML element names
- **Default behavior**: Class name becomes root element: `User` → `<User>...</User>`
- **JAXB alternative**: `jackson-dataformat-xml` is preferred over JAXB for Jackson-based projects
- **`406 Not Acceptable`**: Before adding XML dependency, `Accept: application/xml` returns 406
- **Testing**: Test with `Accept` header in `MockMvc` or Postman to verify both formats work

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Adding XML support to a Spring Boot REST API is just a one-line dependency change. Add jackson-dataformat-xml to your pom.xml and Spring Boot auto-detects it and registers an XML message converter. After that, your existing @RestController methods automatically support both JSON and XML — the client uses the Accept header to choose. Accept: application/json gets JSON, Accept: application/xml gets XML. No changes to your controllers or entities needed. Jackson's regular annotations like @JsonProperty and @JsonIgnore work for both formats. If you need to customize the XML output, there are Jackson XML-specific annotations like @JacksonXmlRootElement to control the root element name.
